To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the replacement of three functional residues in E. coli RNse HI by the corresponding amino acids with amide groups results in the loss of its enzymic activity, that the entire three-dimensional structures of the mutant proteins are not affected, and that very localized conformation changes are observed around the Mg2+-binding site, which are due to the formation of new intermolecular hydrogen bond networks.

the conformational changes around the Mg2+-binding site are induced by the replacements of acidic residues with amide residues in RNase HI, which are completely conserved among reverse transcriptases, and that the conformation of the Mg2+-coordinating side chain in the active site of RNase HI is very important for its enzymic activity.
the replacement of a carboxyl group with an amide group in the active site induces conformational changes around the Mg2+-binding site, which can account for the inactivation of RNase HI.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the elucidation of the structure of RNase HI from E. coli, and the relationship between its structure and its catalytic function.
the structural analysis of ribonucleases.
the elucidation of the catalytic process of E. coli ribonuclease H by means of the x-ray crystallographic study.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the catalytic mechanism of RNase HI involves the following steps: (i) the Mg2+ ion binds to the phosphate group of the scissile phosphate, (ii) the Mg2+-bound scissile phosphate is attacked by a nucleophilic water molecule, (iii) the 5'-hydroxyl group of the cleaved RNA attacks the scissile bond, (iv) a proton from the water molecule is transferred to the 2'-hydroxyl oxygen, and
the Mg2+-binding site of RNase HI is composed of the side chains of Asp10, Glu48, and Asp70, as well as the backbone carbonyl oxygen of Asp10 and the main-chain nitrogen of Glu48.
the Mg(2+) ions play a key role in the catalysis by binding to the carboxyl side-chain oxygen of Asp10 and the phosphate oxygen of the scissile phosphodiester bond.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the three-dimensional structure of RNase HI is highly conserved among various species, and the catalytic mechanism of RNase HI can be explained by a single Mg2+-binding site.
the catalytic residues are located in the vicinity of the metal ion binding site, and the Mg2+ ion is involved in catalysis by stabilizing a transition state of the reaction.

the three-dimensional structure of E. coli ribonuclease H is well preserved in these mutant proteins, and the loss of enzymic activity in these mutants is due to the localized conformational change in the active site.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the structural changes in these mutants are localized around the active site and that the loss of activity is a consequence of these structural perturbations.
the catalytic mechanism of RNase H activity can be explained in terms of the electrostatic interactions among the three acidic residues, Asp10, Glu48, and Asp70.
the three-dimensional structure of RNase HI is not affected by these mutations, which suggests that the three-dimensional fold of this protein is highly stable.
